metaDescription: Five low profile floor jacks for lowered cars and sports cars compared by minimum saddle height, maximum lift, reach, casters and overload protection.
expertTake: The SATA 3-ton ultra-low jack is the best low profile floor jack here, with a 2-11/16 inch minimum height that slides under lowered cars and a dual-piston pump. The TONDA 2.5 ton is the value pick for stock-height sports cars. Skip a low profile jack if you own a truck or a tall SUV, because the short lift range will run out before the frame.
introParagraphs: A low profile floor jack has a short body so the saddle can slip under a car that sits close to the ground. Lowered sedans, sports cars and some modern coupes have jacking points that a standard jack cannot reach without scraping the front bumper or air dam.

The trade for the low entry is usually a shorter maximum lift and a lighter frame. This guide compares five low profile jacks on how low they start, how high they go, how they roll and which safety features they include, and says which suits which car.

products.name: SATA 3-Ton Ultra-Low Profile Steel Floor Jack, 2-11/16 in Height
products.description:
The SATA ultra-low jack has a 2-11/16 inch minimum height, the lowest in this guide, which gets under cars that stop other jacks at the bumper. It carries a 3 ton rating on a thickened steel frame, and every unit is rated to 4.5 tons, 1.5 times its capacity. A dual-piston rapid lift pump reduces handle effort and the number of strokes before the saddle meets the load.

The low entry costs it some lift. It is built for low cars, so it will not reach the high frame of a lifted truck, and the premium price tier is the highest here. Compared with the Bonnlo 3 ton, it starts lower but has a similar 3 ton rating. If your car is truly low, this is the jack that fits.

Expect steel weight, a rubber saddle pad to protect pinch welds and the usual care: oil topped up, ram wiped, stored fully lowered. It is a tool you buy when a standard jack will not fit, and the 2-11/16 inch figure is why. A rubber saddle pad costs little and prevents most pinch weld damage, so fit one even if the jack ships with a bare steel saddle.
products.bestFor: Lowered cars and sports cars with very little ground clearance.
pros: 2-11/16 in minimum slides under lowered cars
3 ton capacity with a 1.5x overload rating
Dual piston pump cuts handle effort
Thickened steel frame is rigid
cons: Heavy steel body is awkward to carry

products.name: Bonnlo 3 Ton Low Profile Floor Jack, 2.95 to 20.1 in
products.description:
The Bonnlo stretches the usual trade: a 2.95 inch minimum height and a 20.1 inch maximum, which spans a lowered coupe and a mid-size SUV with one jack. It has a 6,600 lb rating and a dual-piston pump for quick lifting, with a horizontal hydraulic layout and a heavy-duty frame. It is sold for home garages and workshops, and the range suits trailers as well.

The wide range is the selling point, but a lesser-known brand means you should check parts and warranty terms. Next to the SATA ultra-low it starts a little higher at 2.95 inches, but lifts much higher than any other jack here. If one jack has to serve a sports car and a crossover, this is the choice.

Maintain it like any hydraulic jack: wipe the ram, top up the oil and bleed air if the lift feels soft. Check the saddle pad regularly, and store it lowered. Store it with the handle in its holder so it does not scratch the garage floor or catch a pant leg.
products.bestFor: Households with both a low car and a taller vehicle.
pros: 2.95 in to 20.1 in range covers low cars and SUVs
3 ton rating with a dual piston pump
Fits trailers and MPVs as well
Lower price tier than the SATA
cons: Lesser-known brand with unclear parts support

products.name: Pro-Lift F-767 2 Ton Extra Low Profile Floor Jack, 3-3/8 to 15 in
products.description:
The F-767 is a 2 ton extra low profile jack with a 3-3/8 inch minimum and a 15 inch maximum. Its distinctive feature is a patented bypass device that protects against over-pumping, so the ram cannot be pushed past its safe travel. That makes it a forgiving tool for a home mechanic who is learning to lift a car.

The 2 ton rating is the limit, and 15 inches of lift is enough for a sedan but not a truck. Compared with the Bonnlo 3 ton, it is lighter and cheaper but lifts less. It suits small, low cars where the weight at one end is well under 2 tons.

Ownership is simple: keep the oil topped up, wipe the ram and check the bypass works by pumping to full extension at the start of the season. A brand with a long history is easy to find parts for. Practice the release valve slowly on a hard surface before you trust it with a real lift.
products.bestFor: Small low cars and new home mechanics who want an over-pump safeguard.
pros: 3-3/8 in minimum fits low cars
Patented bypass limits over-pumping
Lighter than 3 ton jacks
Lower price tier
cons: 2 ton rating leaves a thin margin on heavier cars
15 in maximum is short for SUVs

products.name: TONDA 2.5 Ton Low Profile Floor Jack, 3.35 to 14.57 in
products.description:
The TONDA is a 2.5 ton low profile jack with a 3.35 inch minimum height and a 14.57 inch maximum. It uses two large steel wheels and two 360 degree swivel casters for easy positioning, and it is marketed for tire changes and brake jobs on cars. The 5,000 lb rating gives more margin than a 2 ton design.

The maximum height of 14.57 inches is modest, so it is for cars, not trucks. Compared with the Pro-Lift F-767 it offers more capacity and a similar minimum, without the bypass safeguard. It is a good fit for a stock-height sports car or a sedan with a front air dam.

Swivel casters are the feature owners notice: they let you inch the saddle under a bumper without dragging. Keep the casters clean and lightly oiled, and store the jack lowered. Spin the casters by hand once a season, because a seized caster makes the jack twist on the floor.
products.bestFor: Sports cars and sedans for tire and brake work at a low price tier.
pros: 3.35 in minimum fits low cars
2.5 ton rating gives more margin than 2 ton
Swivel casters make positioning easy
Lowest price tier among the picks
cons: 14.57 in maximum is too short for trucks

products.name: AV Steel 2.5 Ton Low Profile Hydraulic Floor Jack, 3.4 to 14.6 in
products.description:
The AV Steel 2.5 ton jack is a low profile model for passenger cars, coupes, hatchbacks and sedans, with a 3.4 inch minimum and 14.6 inch maximum. The maker notes it is not meant for trucks and larger SUVs, and says so plainly, which is helpful guidance. A 5,000 lb rating covers one end of almost any passenger car.

It is nearly identical on paper to the TONDA, with a slightly higher minimum, so the choice comes down to brand support and price. The AV Steel is a plain steel build. Against the SATA, it is far cheaper but has no published overload rating and a single known purpose.

Keep the ram clean, store it lowered and check the oil each season. It is a reasonable choice for a sedan owner who wants a basic low profile jack for the driveway. Mark the lift point on your car with a paint pen so the saddle lands in the same place each time.
products.bestFor: Sedans, hatchbacks and coupes that need a simple low profile jack.
pros: 3.4 in minimum fits most low cars
2.5 ton rating with a steel frame
Maker is clear about intended vehicles
Straightforward design is easy to maintain
cons: Not for trucks or larger SUVs
Nearly identical to cheaper rivals on paper

buyingCriteria.explanation: The minimum saddle height decides whether the jack fits. The SATA lists 2-11/16 inches, the Bonnlo 2.95, the TONDA 3.35, the AV Steel 3.4 and the Pro-Lift 3-3/8. Measure the gap between the jack point and the ground with the car at ride height, and subtract the thickness of your saddle pad. A jack that is half an inch too tall is useless. A cardboard template cut to the height you measure is a cheap way to confirm the fit before ordering.

On low cars the front air dam or bumper blocks the jack before the saddle reaches the jack point. A long chassis or extended reach, as listed for several jacks here, lets you roll the saddle under from the side. Check the distance from the bumper to the jack point on your car, and look for a jack that is long enough to reach. If the air dam is plastic, a short plank under the saddle spreads the load and avoids a crack.

Low profile jacks give up lift for entry height. The AV Steel and TONDA reach about 14.6 inches, the Pro-Lift 15 inches and the Bonnlo 20.1 inches. A 14.6 inch maximum is enough to clear a jack stand under a sedan, but not under a crossover. Add the stand height to your lift point. Always add the stand height to the lift point, not just the jack's maximum, because the stand must sit under the car before you lower it.

A 2 ton Pro-Lift and a 2.5 ton TONDA handle the weight on one end of most sports cars, but a 3 ton jack like the SATA or Bonnlo gives a bigger margin. The SATA lists a 1.5x overload rating, 4.5 tons. Never use the margin as an excuse to skip jack stands. Remember that low cars are often light, so the margin matters less than the entry height.

Dual-piston pumps, on the SATA and Bonnlo, raise the saddle faster, which helps because low profile saddles start far below the car and need many strokes to reach it. A single-piston jack makes you pump a long way before it lifts. For a jack you will use often, dual piston is worth the premium. Count the strokes from fully lowered to the jack point on your own car if you can, since long approach distances multiply the effort.

The TONDA uses two steel wheels and two 360 degree swivel casters, which lets you nudge the saddle into position. Steel low profile jacks weigh 50 to 70 pounds, so rolling and carrying matter. Look for large rear wheels and swivel front casters if you work on a rough garage floor. Wide front casters also make it easier to roll the jack out from under a car that has dropped onto stands.

howWeEvaluated.title: Entry height
howWeEvaluated.description: We ranked jacks by minimum height. The SATA lists 2-11/16 inches, the Bonnlo 2.95, and the others 3.35 to 3.4. Entry height decided most of the placements for low cars. Half an inch decided more placements than any other number.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lift range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared maximum height. The Bonnlo reaches 20.1 inches, and the TONDA and AV Steel reach about 14.6. A longer range earned credit for versatility. A wide range scored higher only if the jack still fit under the lowest car.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at overload ratings and bypass valves. The SATA lists a 1.5x overload rating, and the Pro-Lift has a bypass. Features that protect the ram scored higher. A jack with no published margin was scored cautiously.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pump and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared pump design and casters. Dual pistons on the SATA and Bonnlo raise the saddle fast, and the TONDA has swivel casters. Weight was part of every verdict. Weight was weighed against how often the jack moves.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and support
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched price tier to features and checked brand support. The TONDA and AV Steel are the least expensive, and the SATA is premium. Parts and warranty clarity counted. Clear guidance from the maker was counted as a real plus.

cards.label: 2 to 2.5 ton
cards.text: The Pro-Lift, TONDA and AV Steel are lighter and cheaper. They suit sedans, coupes and sports cars where one end weighs well under their rating.

cards.label: 3 ton
cards.text: The SATA and Bonnlo give a bigger margin and suit heavier cars and crossovers. They cost more and weigh more, but handle a wider range of vehicles.

howToChoose.note: Choose 3 ton if you may own a heavier car later, and 2.5 ton if you are sure of a light one.

howToChoose.subheading: For a Lowered Sports Car Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A minimum height under 3 inches, a long reach and a rubber or wide saddle that will not mar the jack point. Plan to use a plank or ramps if the front lip is very low.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The SATA 3-Ton ultra-low fits best at 2-11/16 inches. The Bonnlo is the alternative if you also own a taller vehicle.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your car is very low or you lift often. The SATA's height and overload rating, or the Bonnlo's range, are worth the premium.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your car is stock height and the jack is for seasonal use. The TONDA or AV Steel is sufficient.

maintenance.why: Low oil causes soft lifts. Use jack oil with the ram retracted. Skipping this is the usual reason a jack will not hold.
Grit scores the seals. Wipe clean and store lowered. Sand any surface rust off the ram before it pits the seal.
Air in the lines makes lifts soft. Open the release valve and pump the handle. Pump slowly with the valve open to avoid spraying oil.
Dry casters bind and make positioning harder. A rusty caster is the first sign of storage in a damp corner.
A worn pad damages pinch welds and can slip. Replace the pad if you can see the steel through the rubber.

faq.q: What is the lowest floor jack?
faq.a: Among these, the SATA ultra-low lists 2-11/16 inches. Many low profile jacks start between 3 and 4 inches. Check your car's ground clearance at the jack point before choosing. A tape measure and ten minutes beat a return shipment.

faq.q: Can I use a low profile jack on an SUV?
faq.a: Usually not. Low profile jacks give up maximum lift, so a 14.6 inch jack may not reach an SUV's frame. The Bonnlo's 20.1 inch maximum is an exception, but check your lift point. Check the maker's listed vehicle types before buying.

faq.q: Do I need jack stands with a low profile jack?
faq.a: Yes. A floor jack lifts, and jack stands hold the load. Place stands at the correct support points before working under the car. Use stands rated above the car weight.
On a low profile jack, yes. The saddle starts far below the car and needs many strokes to reach it. A dual piston pump cuts the strokes. Count the strokes once and you will see the difference.

faq.q: How do I avoid scratching the front bumper?
faq.a: Use a long jack that can reach from the side, or place a plank or ramp under the front tires. A rubber saddle pad protects the jack point. A small plank is a cheap tool that saves a bumper.

faq.q: How long will a low profile jack last?
faq.a: A well-kept steel jack can last many years. Keep the oil topped up and store it lowered. A cheap jack with no overload rating may show seal wear sooner. Replace the jack if it leaks on the floor.
